name: Diego Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer for a builders' merchant supply company. We distribute fixings, screws, hinges, hand tools and power tools to about forty trade counters. I look after the fixings range, which sounds dull, but it's eleven thousand product lines. My day is checking the reorder report, ringing suppliers in the morning, and sorting out whatever went wrong overnight with deliveries.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your way of working? Any tools you rely on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A notebook and the phone. I write every supplier promise down with a date, and I chase it on that date. The company keeps sending emails about AI training and I keep deleting them, to be honest. I don't see what a chatbot knows about a coach bolt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd expect, really. Most new systems at work end up doing about half of what the salesman promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like every other system we've had: loads of fuss, small difference. At football on Tuesday I'd joke that the robots still can't find a bag of M8 nuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm comfortable. Pay's fine for what it is, and I've got about three months of rent saved. There are other merchants around here if this place ever went wrong, so I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much different. I'd keep my notebook, keep the same suppliers, and keep putting a bit aside each month. If the company made me use some AI reorder feature, I'd use it, but I'd still check it against my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. It's just a Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you even in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit. My landlord sold the last place I lived and I had to move in a month. I'd like to buy one day, but on one salary that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made it compulsory, fine. But I'd want them to show me it works on our real stock first, not on some demo. My notebook has never lost a supplier promise.

say: AI is like **every other system**: lots of fuss, small difference.
I'd joke that robots still can't find a **bag of M8 nuts**.
think: I'm **comfortable**: pay's fine and I have about three months' rent saved.
There are **other merchants** nearby if this place ever went wrong.
do: Keep my **notebook** and the same suppliers.
Keep putting **a bit aside** each month.
Use any compulsory **AI feature** but check it against my notes.
S0.quote: My notebook has never lost a supplier promise.
fieldNote: Diego is **settled** and sceptical, judging AI by past systems that underdelivered.
His only quiet worry is **renting alone** on one salary.
He'll comply with tools but **double-check** everything by hand.

steps.text: Keep chasing suppliers with the paper notebook
Keep saving a little each month toward a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying's on that list. That's me. I don't love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see it work first. Out loud I'd be fair about it: some of the reorder stuff probably could be automated, it's just counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm exposed. I'm not the quickest with new tech, and if the company wants three buyers who run software instead of six who use the phone, I know which group I'd be in. The suppliers like me, but suppliers don't decide headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the AI training this time, even though I'd hate it. I'd cut back, no new car, and get the savings up from three months to six. And I'd quietly look at other merchants nearby, maybe a branch manager job where I'm out on the counter with customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like being picked last for a team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said suppliers like you. Doesn't that count for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It counts until the software gets a better price. Suppliers will like whoever pays them. I'm not daft about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a branch job look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a trade counter, talking to builders all day, sorting their orders. It's more hands-on and people still want a face. The pay's similar, the hours are worse, early starts.

say: Let's **see it work** on our real stock first.
Some **reorder work** probably could be automated; it's just counting.
think: I'm **exposed**, because I'm slow with new tech.
**Suppliers like me**, but suppliers don't decide headcount.
Three buyers running **software** would replace six on the phone.
do: Go to the **AI training** this time, despite hating it.
Skip the new car and raise savings to **six months**.
Look for a **branch manager** job on a trade counter.
S1.quote: The suppliers like me, but suppliers don't decide headcount.
fieldNote: Diego's public fairness hides a **private fear** of being cut.
He'd swallow his dislike and **attend training**, a big step for him.
The **trade counter** appeals because customers still want a face.

steps.text: Sign up for the company's AI training course
Skip the new car and save toward six months' rent
Apply for branch manager jobs at local trade counters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Then I'm done. There's no version of that where I keep a buying job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and I'd say the government needs to slow it down. I'm not a political person, but I'd want someone in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. My work is phones and spreadsheets. The only hands-on part is when I go to the warehouse to look at damaged stock, and that's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd apply for counter jobs and warehouse supervisor jobs, because robots take three more years for those. I'd stop all spending except rent and food. I'd also ask my uncle, who runs a small building firm, whether he'd take me on as a labourer or estimator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. I'm not built for that much change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2031, when robots come for warehouse work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea. I'd have three years on a counter, then the same problem again. Maybe by then I'd learn a trade with my uncle, plastering or tiling, the fiddly stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to. My rent's my biggest cost. I could go back to my mum's spare room for a year if it got bad. I wouldn't like it at twenty-nine, but I'd do it.

say: It's **mad**, and the government needs to **slow it down**.
I'm not political, but I'd want **someone in charge**.
think: I'm **done** as a buyer within two years.
My work is **phones and spreadsheets**, with almost nothing hands-on.
do: Apply for **counter and warehouse** supervisor jobs in month one.
Stop all spending except **rent and food**.
Ask my uncle about **labouring or estimating** work.
S2.quote: I could go back to my mum's spare room for a year if it got bad. I wouldn't like it at twenty-nine, but I'd do it.
fieldNote: Diego sees **no way to keep** a buying job and says so flatly.
He'd lean on **family**: his uncle's building firm and his mum's spare room.
The **robot delay** gives him three years, which he sees as a stopgap.

steps.text: Apply for trade counter and warehouse supervisor jobs
Cut spending to rent and food only
Ask his uncle for work at the building firm
Move back to his mum's spare room if money runs low

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. Still fast, but at least I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better start training people now. It's common sense, not left or right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, just later. I'd have time to learn a trade properly, maybe with my uncle. I'm better with my hands than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep buying and save hard, toward six months. In the second year I'd start an evening course in tiling or plastering. By year four I'd want to be working part-time with my uncle's firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but it's a slower alarm. More like a smoke detector beeping in another room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you hate new things. Is a trade new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's new, but it's real. You can see a wall you've plastered. I'd rather learn that than learn to babysit a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if robots come for plastering in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd hope the old houses round here are awkward enough to need a person for a while. Nobody really knows.

say: We'd better **start training** people now, while there are five years.
Training is **common sense**, not a left or right thing.
think: It's the **same ending** for buying, just later.
I'm **better with my hands** than people think.
Five years is time to learn a **trade properly**.
do: Keep buying and save toward **six months**.
Start an **evening course** in tiling or plastering in year two.
Work **part-time** with my uncle's firm by year four.
feel: Like a **smoke detector** beeping in another room.
S3.quote: You can see a wall you've plastered. I'd rather learn that than learn to babysit a computer.
fieldNote: Diego expects to **lose the job** either way, so his worry stays high.
He'd pick a **trade** over learning AI, reflecting his dislike of screens.
His centre view frames training as **common sense**.

steps.text: Save toward six months of rent while still buying
Start an evening tiling or plastering course in year two
Work part-time for his uncle's building firm by year four

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a different life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's manageable if people get on with it. Plenty of time to learn something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still worry, because I know I put things off. But ten years means I could finish a trade, get some years in, maybe even buy a small flat before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying for a few years and keep saving. In year three I'd start a plastering course. I'd keep an eye on the company, and if they started cutting buyers early I'd move sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. It's far enough off to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you put things off. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having a date. If my uncle said start in year five, I'd be there. I'm good at keeping promises to other people, just not to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to buy a flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. A small one, near my mum. Having a roof I own would make the rest of it less frightening.

say: It's **manageable** if people get on with it.
With ten years there's **plenty of time** to learn something else.
think: I still **worry**, because I know I put things off.
Ten years lets me finish a trade and maybe **buy a small flat**.
do: Keep buying and **saving** for a few years.
Start a **plastering course** in year three.
Move sooner if the company **cuts buyers early**.
S4.quote: I'm good at keeping promises to other people, just not to myself.
fieldNote: Diego still expects the **buying job to go**, so worry stays, but it's planned.
He knows his **procrastination** and plans around commitments to others.
Owning a **small flat** would steady him.

steps.text: Keep buying and saving for the next few years
Start a plastering course in year three
Save for a small flat near his mum

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time to learn anything and nothing to fall back on but family. What would help is cheap evening trade courses and some kind of income while you retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how people actually learn. I can't learn from a video. I need someone to show me with my hands.

headlineQuote: I don't see what a chatbot knows about a coach bolt.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old buyer** of fixings for a builders' merchant supplier, living alone and renting.
He trusts his **notebook** and phone and has never used AI tools.
He's **pragmatic**, wanting training framed as common sense rather than politics.
He moves from calm to **alarmed** as AGI timelines shorten.
His fallback is **family**: his uncle's building firm and a trade like plastering.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to learn anything new.
